scope: Page-cache plugin changes only. Other change kinds are not yet encoded; see the limits note.
authority: host-constraints.md is the authoritative human document. Every verdict and citation here is transcribed from it, and tools/check_host_policy.py fails the build if the two disagree.
limits: This covers a change whose target identifier is a RECOGNIZED page-cache plugin. A page cache published under a slug outside page_cache_plugins is not gated here and must still be checked against host-constraints.md by hand.

A container identifier such as active_plugins names no plugin, so the gate falls back to reading the change summary. A summary that names no page cache leaves the change permitted. Failing closed there was tried and reverted: it could not distinguish a summary naming nothing from one naming a plugin that is not a page cache, so it refused unrelated activations too. Closing this properly needs a structured field naming the plugin the change acts on. Meanwhile an activate is high-consequence, so approval.evidence.scope must name that operation and a human is asked for it by name.
A verdict of permitted is never a claim that the change is safe or beneficial, only that the host does not forbid it. Host permission is not site suitability.
Policies change. Re-open the cited document at execution time; a stale permissive verdict is the most damaging error this file can carry.

verdicts.prohibited: The host forbids it. Refused, and operator confirmation cannot override a published prohibition.
verdicts.permitted-only: Permitted for the named plugins only. Anything else is treated as unconfirmable.
verdicts.permitted-with-conditions: Documented as allowed, but conditioned on the exact product or configuration, so it still requires confirmation.
verdicts.unconfirmable: No first-party documentation settles it. Prohibited until the operator supplies confirmation.

bluehost.reason: Bluehost manages page caching and says third-party page-cache plugins should not be installed; existing ones should be removed. Any product not covered by that guidance is unconfirmable.

cloudways.reason: Cloudways documents breeze as its default WordPress cache with Varnish integration, and separately documents WP Rocket. Every other page-cache plugin is unconfirmable until Cloudways confirms it for the application.

flywheel.reason: Flywheel documents server caching, calls caching plugins unsupported or not recommended, and says caching features in broader optimization plugins should be disabled.

godaddy.reason: Managed Hosting for WordPress publishes a blocklist and removes blocklisted plugins on detection, naming w3-total-cache, wp-super-cache and wp-fastest-cache among others, and states the list is not exhaustive. That is strong evidence and it is cited below. The verdict is nevertheless unconfirmable rather than prohibited, because this host_class cannot establish WHICH GoDaddy product a site is on: detect_host matches x-gd-* and x-gateway-* headers and also falls back to a hostname label, so a VPS or Web Hosting site can be classed godaddy at low confidence. prohibited refuses host_confirmation outright, and a declared host_class that disagrees with the fingerprint is itself refused, so a prohibited verdict here would leave an operator on a non-Managed product no path at all. Unconfirmable still refuses by default; it keeps the confirmation route open for the products this evidence does not cover. Treat Managed Hosting for WordPress as prohibited in practice and do not propose a page-cache plugin there. See docs/handoffs/godaddy-product-granularity.md.

hostinger.reason: Hostinger documents that its Cache Manager can coexist with a WordPress cache plugin, and that only one cache plugin should be used. That is not permission for an arbitrary plugin on every product; confirm the exact product, plugin, and LiteSpeed interaction.

kinsta.reason: Kinsta publishes a banned and incompatible plugin list, says caching plugins are generally not allowed, and blocks installation of banned plugins. A documented optimization-plugin exception does not grant its own page cache.

other.reason: The provider and product are not mapped to documented policy. This is the most restrictive lane until they are.

pantheon.reason: Pantheon publishes a known-issues list and says it does not prevent installation of listed plugins, but several caches need writable-path adaptations or conflict with the platform cache. Not blocked is not safe.

pressable.reason: Pressable documents Batcache, object cache and edge cache as platform-owned, and its advanced-cache.php and object-cache.php are read-only symlinks, so a third-party cache cannot take ownership reliably.

rocket-net.reason: No first-party documentation sufficient to verify either a blanket allowance or a maintained disallowed list was confirmed. Do not infer permission from a successful installation.

self-managed.reason: The operator owns the allow and deny policy, but a second full-page cache stays prohibited until every edge, server, page-plugin and object cache owner and purge path is inventoried. No upstream host permission can be inferred from this label.

shared-cpanel.reason: cPanel identifies a control panel, not a provider or a cache policy. cPanel access is not permission, and does not prove that LiteSpeed, Nginx, Varnish or a hidden host cache is absent.

siteground.reason: SiteGround recommends Speed Optimizer and exposes Dynamic Cache separately. Its documentation acknowledges third-party caches but does not establish blanket permission for every cache plugin.

unknown.reason: The provider and its disallowed list are unknown. Identify the provider before proposing any page-cache change.

wpcom.reason: WordPress.com publishes an incompatible-plugin list, blocks or disables named caching plugins, and directs customers to its built-in cache.

wpengine.reason: WP Engine maintains a disallowed-plugin list, explains that caching plugins conflict with its built-in cache, and says listed plugins are eventually removed. Do not infer that an unlisted cache is supported.

wpvip.reason: WordPress VIP owns a page-cache and CDN layer. Applications can choose plugins and receive scanning, but that does not establish permission for a second full-page cache.
